pages.title: Demo App product overview
pages.summary: Customer-facing reporting application used as the pinned demo product.

blocks.p: Demo App is a reporting application for a fictional customer, the Lakeside Retail Cooperative. It renders saved report views, exports them, and keeps the export history auditable. Everything on this page is pinned demo data: the product, its customer, its numbers, and its history are invented for the demonstration.

rows: Saved views, filters, and column layout for recurring reports.
CSV export with deterministic escaping and timezone handling.
Retention window, download receipts, and deletion proof.
Keyboard-first board operation and a contrast baseline.

ul: The board carries one delivery thread: plan the reports export, build it, review it, decide it, and document the outcome.
The [Dossier index](dossiers/README.md) holds the six documents that explain why the work looks the way it does.
The [reporting domain](product/10-reporting-domain.md) explains the four concepts every card and document refers to.
The [system map](system/10-system-map.md) shows which parts belong to Demo App and which belong to Demo Platform.
Recorded runs, tokens, and diffs are replayed fixtures. No agent is editing a repository while you browse.

blocks.note: Pinned demo data. The cooperative, the report fixtures, and the metrics on this page are invented for the demo instance.

pages.title: Reporting domain
pages.summary: The four concepts every Demo App card and Dossier refers to.

blocks.p: A report is a named selection over the cooperative's sales fixtures. A preset freezes a filter set for a team, an export job renders one preset into a file, and a retention window decides how long that file stays downloadable. Four concepts are enough to read every card on the board.

rows: Columns, sort order, and the active filter set.
A report always resolves to a deterministic row order.
A named filter set shared inside one team.
A preset never changes an existing export.
One rendered file plus its receipt.
A finished job is immutable; a repeat is a new job.
How long a rendered file stays downloadable.
Expiry deletes the file and keeps the receipt.

ul: A preset can be renamed without rewriting history, because an export keeps its own resolved filter set.
A retention change never edits a receipt, so the export history stays complete ([DEMO-17](task:DEMO-17)).
Team presets are the reason export presets are a card of their own ([DEMO-16](task:DEMO-16)).

rows: A personal report with its filters.

pages.title: System map
pages.summary: Which component owns which part of the reporting flow, and where Demo Platform begins.

blocks.p: Demo App is a small client, a report API, and an export worker. Demo Platform sits behind it as a supporting service. The split exists so cross-project navigation in this demo shows real structure instead of two unrelated card lists.

rows: Board, filters, export dialog, and download list.
Report resolution, preset storage, export job intake.
Renders a job into a file and writes the receipt.
Product and store catalog reads for report labels.
Health endpoint and structured request logging.

ol: The client submits a preset and a date range to the report API.
The report API resolves labels through the Demo Platform catalog service.
An export job is queued; the client subscribes to its progress.
The export worker renders the file, writes the receipt, and marks the job complete.
The retention window starts when the receipt is written.

ul: Demo App never reads the catalog store directly; it goes through the catalog service.
Demo Platform never renders a report file. It only answers catalog, health, and logging calls.
The catalog cache policy belongs to Demo Platform, not to the report API. It is documented in the Demo Platform Wiki, which the project switcher reaches in one step.

pages.title: Cache policy
pages.summary: Catalog cache windows, invalidation, and the one guarantee callers may rely on.

blocks.p: Catalog reads dominate the traffic, so they are cached. The policy is small enough that a caller can reason about staleness without reading the implementation.

A caller that reads twice within one request sees the same value. Nothing else is promised: a cache is a latency tool here, not a consistency mechanism. The delivery for this behavior is [PLAT-3](task:PLAT-3).

blocks.note: Pinned demo data. Windows, entries, and guarantees are invented for the demo instance.

pages.summary: The bounded response path for a catalog or logging incident in this demo product.

items.title: Reusable dashboard filters
items.summary: Shape the filter reuse problem before proposing a solution: friction, goals, constraints, and the next evidence step.
items.lead: People rebuild the same filter set several times a day. This document collects what we observed, what a good outcome would be, and what we still need to find out. No option is chosen yet.

ul: A weekly review rebuilds the same four filters on three different reports.
Filters are lost when the report is reopened from a link, so the link is not shareable in practice.
Two teams use different names for the same filter set, which makes a handover a translation exercise.

rows: Reopen yesterday's view without rebuilding it.
A returning user reaches the same rows in one action.
Share a view with a colleague.
A shared link resolves to the same rows for both people.
A filter set has one name that survives a handover.

ul: A saved filter must not change the result of an export that already exists.
The board must stay usable without saved filters; this is an accelerator, not a prerequisite.
Nothing here may widen what a report can read.

ol: Do people want a personal saved view, a team-shared preset, or both? The two imply different ownership and deletion rules.
Is the filter set or the column layout the thing people actually want back?

blocks.p: Watch one weekly review end to end and record how many filter rebuilds happen, which of them are identical, and where the reviewer looks first. That measurement decides whether this becomes a preset feature, a link-state fix, or nothing.

blocks.note: No option is presented as chosen. This document stays in shaping until the observation above exists.

lifecycleHistory.note: Opened after the third repeated filter rebuild in one weekly review.

items.title: Export retention and privacy
items.summary: Compare 7, 30, and 90-day retention for rendered exports and leave the policy and deletion-proof questions open for an operator.
items.lead: A rendered export is a copy of customer data with a lifetime. This document compares three windows, records what each one costs, recommends 30 days, and leaves both open decisions to the operator.

blocks.p: Two questions are open. The first sets the default retention window. The second decides whether a customer can request proof that an expired export was deleted. They are separable: a short window without deletion proof is a defensible position, and so is a longer window with proof.

rows: A missed download costs a rerun.
Smallest copy surface; least to explain to a customer.
Covers a full monthly reporting cycle.
Moderate copy surface; matches the current default.
Covers a quarter with no reruns.
Largest copy surface; the hardest to justify without proof of deletion.

blocks.p: Keep 30 days. It matches the reporting cycle people actually work in, and the storage cost is not the binding constraint. The stronger argument for 7 days is privacy, and deletion proof addresses that concern more directly than a shorter window does.

decision.question: Which retention window becomes the durable default?

options.label: 7 days
options.summary: Smallest copy surface, reruns become normal.

decision.comment: Optional note for the retention decision

items.title: Reports export release
items.summary: The chosen implementation direction for the CSV export, its slice boundaries, review criteria, and the current delivery state.
items.lead: The reports export ships as four bounded slices with one operator decision at the end. This document holds the direction; the card points beside it are projected live from the board and are not copied into this text.

blocks.p: Render exports server-side from the same report resolution the board uses, stream progress into the activity feed, and keep the file immutable once its receipt is written. The alternative, rendering in the client, was rejected because a large export would then depend on one browser session staying open. Deterministic cell escaping and timezone handling were already delivered and reviewed before this decision; they are the reason the release question is now about the remaining four slices only.

items.summary: The original decision, the delivered shortcut map, the accessibility proof, and the measured outcome, kept as durable documentation.
items.lead: Board navigation had to work without a pointer. The work is finished and its references are terminal, so this Dossier is no longer a decision surface: it is the page someone reads when they ask why the shortcuts are what they are.

blocks.p: Use single-key shortcuts scoped to the focused lane instead of a global chord scheme. Chords were rejected because they collide with browser and assistive-technology bindings, and because a single key is discoverable from a visible hint row.

items.title: Legacy notification banner experiment
items.summary: Why the persistent notification banner was discarded and what replaced it, with the archive receipt that closed the proposal.
items.lead: A persistent banner was proposed to surface product notices at the top of the board. It was built as an experiment, measured, and discarded. This document exists so the idea is not proposed again without new evidence.

ul: It duplicated the activity feed: every notice it showed was already one scroll away, in context.
It performed poorly in the accessibility review: it took focus on mount and pushed the board down on every notice.
It was superseded by an inline status pattern that puts the notice next to the thing it is about.
